title: In-plane magnetic field control of anomalous Hall response enabled by magnetic anisotropy engineering
authors: J. C. Rodriguez E., E. De Biasi, J. I. Facio, D. Salomoni, S. Auffret, R. C. Sousa, I. L. Prejbeanu, A. Bruchhausen, J. Curiale, L. Avilés-Félix
abstract: Engineering magnetic anisotropy provides a powerful route to control magnetization orientation and unlock emerging functionalities in opto-spintronic and current-driven devices. Beyond its role in magnetization reversal, the effective anisotropy can strongly influence the magnetotransport response, offering an additional degree of freedom to tune new device functionalities. In this work, we report a magnetotransport study of a ferrimagnetic [Tb/Co]$_{\times 5}$ multilayer grown with a Tb thickness gradient, whose wedge-shaped tilts the uniaxial anisotropy axis slightly away from the film normal. Anomalous Hall resistivity measurements from 80 K to 300 K reveal a spin reorientation transition, while the angular dependence of the magnetotransport responses exposes the crucial role of the tilted anisotropy. A simplified macrospin model reproduces the full angular response across the transition and shows that the observed anomalous Hall effect when the in-plane magnetic field is applied originates from the tilt of the uniaxial anisotropy axis, which supplies a built-in symmetry-breaking mechanism, enabling in-plane field control over the out-of-plane anomalous Hall response, sign included. These findings establish tilted magnetic anisotropy as a promising route toward Hall effect-based sensor applications and highlight Tb/Co multilayers as a versatile platform for anisotropy-engineered spintronic devices.
summary: This work reports on magnetotransport studies of Tb/Co multilayers where the magnetic anisotropy has been engineered to be tilted. The key finding is that this built-in tilt breaks symmetry, enabling the anomalous Hall effect to be controlled by applying an in-plane magnetic field. This establishes the material as a promising platform for advanced Hall effect sensors.
main_problem: The study aims to control the anomalous Hall response in magnetic multilayers using an in-plane magnetic field by engineering the magnetic anisotropy.
main_result: The anomalous Hall effect observed under an in-plane field originates from the tilt of the uniaxial anisotropy axis, which breaks symmetry and allows for in-plane field control over the out-of-plane AHE sign.
method: Magnetotransport measurements of anomalous Hall resistivity ($ho_{xy}$) and longitudinal resistivity ($ho_{xx}$) are performed as a function of external magnetic field angle and temperature.
model_or_system: The physical system is a ferrimagnetic [Tb/Co] multilayer grown with a Tb thickness gradient, inducing a wedge-shaped tilt in the uniaxial anisotropy axis. The analysis is supported by a simplified macrospin model.
key_observables: Anomalous Hall resistivity ($ho_{xy}$), longitudinal resistivity ($ho_{xx}$), coercive field ($H_C$), and angular dependence of transport coefficients.
important_parameters: Temperature range (80 K to 300 K), in-plane field orientation ($\phi_H$), and the degree of anisotropy tilt.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a simplified macrospin model, and the AHE is assumed to be dominated by the Co sublattice in the measured temperature window.
figures_summary: Figures show $ho_{xy}$ loops revealing spin reorientation transitions, and angular dependence measurements ($ho_{xx}, ho_{xy}$ vs. angle) demonstrating the influence of the tilted anisotropy.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates magnetotransport responses ($ho_{xx}, ho_{xy}$) under both out-of-plane and in-plane field rotations, using angular dependence analysis and comparison with a macrospin model to pinpoint the role of the anisotropy tilt.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of using engineered anisotropy to control symmetry-breaking mechanisms that govern transport responses (like AHE) has parallels in controlling quantum states or coupling strengths in quantum devices.
